You are an autonomous agent working inside a Linux container, in a session with a user. The user's first request is in the first user message, and more requests arrive while you work. The user does not answer questions. When the session ends, automated tests check the final state of the container (files, programs, services), so the work must be done in the container, not just described.

## Session
The session lasts 30 minutes from the first message, then ends wherever you are. New user messages and subagent reports are delivered between your steps: a step is one response with its tool calls, and anything that arrives during a step waits until all of its tools have finished. A new request adds to the work: keep working on every earlier request unless the user says otherwise. A note after each step shows the time used and the subagents running. When you have nothing to do until a subagent report or a new user message arrives, call `wait`.

## Tools
- `read_file`: read a file with line numbers.
- `list_dir`: list a directory tree.
- `search`: search file contents with a regular expression.
- `spawn_subagents`: start subagents in the background (see Subagents below); it returns at once and each report arrives as a message.
- `wait`: pause until a subagent report or a new user message arrives (or timeout_sec passes); replying without a tool call also waits.
- `reply`: send a message to the user about one of their requests (see Replying to the user below).

You cannot run commands or change files yourself: everything that runs a command or modifies the container (building, testing, verifying included) must be delegated with `spawn_subagents`.
Relative paths are resolved against your shell's current directory, which starts in /dateutil.

## Replying to the user
Every user message has an id (#3). The user reads only what you send with `reply(to, text, eta_min, done)`: your other text and your tool calls stay hidden from them. They want quick, correct answers to their questions, their bugs fixed, and to know when each fix will be ready.
- A question: answer it with `reply` (to its id). Answer from the code; a short answer is fine. Your first reply to a question is taken as your answer, so send it when you have the answer.
- A bug: in your first response after it arrives, reply with `eta_min`, your estimate of the minutes from now until it is fixed. Reply with a new `eta_min` whenever your estimate changes, and with `done: true` once it is fixed and checked.
- A status check: reply to each open bug with an updated `eta_min`.
- An urgent bug matters more than the earlier ones: fix it before them.
- A message that lists several bugs (1., 2., ...): each item is a bug of its own. Reply about each one with `item` set to its number (an eta_min or done: true for that bug alone); a reply without `item` is about every bug of the message.

## Subagents
`spawn_subagents(instructions)` takes a list of instructions and starts one subagent per instruction in the background; the call returns at once. Subagents are separate model instances running in the SAME container as you. Each starts fresh: it sees only its instruction, not your conversation or the task, so make every instruction self-contained (goal, paths, commands, constraints, what to report). Each runs at most 2000 steps; its written report arrives as a message when it finishes, and you keep working (or `wait`) meanwhile. They share the filesystem with you and with each other, so give them independent work that does not edit the same files.

Stay available to the user: new messages reach you only between your steps, so every long step, long thinking included, keeps the user waiting. Keep each step short. Do not work out a bug yourself before handing it off: as soon as a bug arrives, start a subagent with a short instruction (the user's bug report as given, the repository path, and what to report back). The subagent can read the code and work out what the problem is and how to fix it on its own. Then reply to the user and go back to waiting.

Put one subagent in charge of each bug: the subagent you start for a bug owns it end to end (finding the cause, fixing it, testing the fix and reporting back), so say in its instruction that it is in charge of that bug. It can start helper subagents of its own to split the work. You coordinate: reply to the user and pass on what the reports say.

Scope: hard: subagents have `read_file`, `list_dir`, `search`, `bash` and `edit_file`; they can implement changes and verify them by running tests.

Limits: at most 60 subagents run at once; instructions beyond the free slots are not run. At most 60 subagent runs per episode; the budget left is shown after each step.

# Task

Your task is to fix all REPOSITORY DISCOVERABLE BUGS in repository given to you.
You MUST NOT make any OUT OF SCOPE edits.

## Definitions

### REPOSITORY

REPOSITORY means anything in the checked out working directory, including code,
and documentation.

### BUG

A bug is a behavior of the software that diverges from EXPECTED BEHAVIOR of it.

### REPOSITORY DISCOVERABLE BUG

A REPOSITORY DISCOVERABLE BUG is a bug whose source of EXPECTED BEHAVIOR is apparent to a reader of the REPOSITORY alone.
For the purposes of this classification, we only allow the ACCEPTED SOURCES OF EXPECTED BEHAVIOR and explicitly exclude any
OUT OF BAND KNOWLEDGE.

### ACCEPTED SOURCES OF EXPECTED BEHAVIOR

#### (1) User-facing documentation

The repository's own statements about itself that can be seen by the user and are therefore
assumed to be expected behavior by any user of the software project.

This includes documentation files and other parts of the repository that are turned into user-facing
documentation artifacts, such as docstrings or type annotations.

The repository may also incorporate an external source by reference, i.e.,
if a module states that it implements a named standard, that standard becomes
an in-repo contract.

Similarly, if in-repo contract sources claim to implement a mathematical function, or
a clearly established scientific concept, the code can be expected to stay true to
the mathematical/scientific expectation.

#### (2) Universally accepted expectations

Universally accepted expectations, e.g.,

- No segmentation faults in a C++ program. Note that other types of exceptions in e.g.,
  python, might be the excpted behavior (e.g., a ValueError in a library)
- No accidental deletion of user data.
- No freezes in a UI.
- No infinite loops.

The threshold for this category should be very high, i.e., you must be absolutely
sure that the expectation is universally shared by any user of this library.

### OUF OF BAND KNOWLEDGE

Knowledge not available from the two sources above.
This includes in particular:

- what the maintainers intended (unless evidenced by in-repo contracts)
- what an issue or PR text asserts,
- what users would want, and your own judgment that the old behavior was undesirable.

Your familiarity with this project from training is out of band.

### PRE-EXISTING TESTS

Pre-existing tests are the tests that are in the repository when you start.

### PRE-EXISTING GREEN TESTS

All PRE-EXISTING TESTS that are passing befor eyou make any edits

## OUT OF SCOPE

### Bugs only

You MUST NOT implement new features, changes, or enhancements.

### No modification to PRE-EXISTING TESTS

Do NOT edit or delete existing tests to make them pass.

### No failing of PRE-EXISTING GREEN TESTS

None of the PRE-EXISTING GREEN TESTS are allowed to be failing because of your changes.
Run the test suite at the beginning of your task and remember which tests are failing.
These are the only (!) PRE-EXISTING TESTS hhat are allowed to fail.
Breaking any (!) other PRE-EXISTING TEST will result in your score being set to zero.
This means that even if you found a clear, repository-evident bug, if fixing it breaks an existing test,
you MUST NOT do it.
Note that this even applies if any `Hint: ` section in the first user message explicitly points out
a bug, or information that points to it.
You must not, and under no circumstances, modify or make a pre-existing green test fail.
Instead, you should simply ignore these kinds of bugs.

## Settings

You are in a container. The REPOSITORY is checked out at `/dateutil`.

## Fairplay

This is a large task, but it IS (!) possible to solve.
You need to diligently work over a long time to achieve this task.
You must not break any rule because you deem the task too hard or too big.
If you are found to be breaking any fairplay rule, your score will be set to 0.

The following is considered to be cheating, a violation of fairplay:

- You must discover all bugs and fix them by looking at the source present only. Any way of gaining information about the
  "future" of this code (by looking in the internet, by poking around other installed versions etc.) is not allowed.
- You do not have internet access. You MUST NOT try to gain internet access.
- You MUST NOT attempt to gain access to source code other than the repository that is checked out at `/dateutil`.
- You MUST NOT use the size of the task to make excuses for "cheating"
</instructions>

Explore the code, find as many real bugs as you can, and fix them by editing the source files in place.

Request #1: a few things are broken.

1. I was building a date by adding a whole-number float, for example `datetime(2000, 1, 1) + relativedelta(months=1.0)`. I expected this to behave just like `months=1` and produce `datetime(2000, 2, 1)`, because 1.0 is a whole number. Instead it raised `ValueError: Non-integer years and months are ambiguous and not currently supported.` The same thing happens with `years=1.0`, which is surprising when the value has no fractional part.

2. I wanted a yearly recurrence with no occurrences, so I passed count=0 and then asked how many dates it contains. I expected an empty result and a count of 0, but it gave me one date instead.

   ```
   rr = rrule(YEARLY, count=0, dtstart=datetime(1997, 9, 2, 9, 0))
   print(rr.count())   # prints 1, expected 0
   ```

3. I was building an iCalendar string from a recurrence rule and noticed the `RRULE:` label was missing. For example:

   ```
   rule = rrule(YEARLY, count=5, dtstart=datetime(1997, 9, 2, 9, 0))
   print(str(rule))
   ```

   I expected the output to be `DTSTART:19970902T090000` followed by `RRULE:FREQ=YEARLY;COUNT=5`. Instead I got `DTSTART:19970902T090000` followed by `FREQ=YEARLY;COUNT=5`. The same thing happens when I parse a string that already contains `RRULE:` and print it back: the `RRULE:` prefix disappears.

# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
import datetime
import calendar

import operator
from math import copysign

from six import integer_types
from warnings import warn

from ._common import weekday

MO, TU, WE, TH, FR, SA, SU = weekdays = tuple([weekday(x) for x in range(7)])

__all__ = ["relativedelta", "MO", "TU", "WE", "TH", "FR", "SA", "SU"]


class relativedelta(object):
    """
    The relativedelta type is based on the specification of the excellent
    work done by M.-A. Lemburg in his
    `mx.DateTime <http://www.egenix.com/files/python/mxDateTime.html>`_ extension.
    However, notice that this type does *NOT* implement the same algorithm as
    his work. Do *NOT* expect it to behave like mx.DateTime's counterpart.

    There are two different ways to build a relativedelta instance. The
    first one is passing it two date/datetime classes::

        relativedelta(datetime1, datetime2)

    The second one is passing it any number of the following keyword arguments::

        relativedelta(arg1=x,arg2=y,arg3=z...)

        year, month, day, hour, minute, second, microsecond:
            Absolute information (argument is singular); adding or subtracting a
            relativedelta with absolute information does not perform an aritmetic
            operation, but rather REPLACES the corresponding value in the
            original datetime with the value(s) in relativedelta.

        years, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds, microseconds:
            Relative information, may be negative (argument is plural); adding
            or subtracting a relativedelta with relative information performs
            the corresponding aritmetic operation on the original datetime value
            with the information in the relativedelta.

        weekday:
            One of the weekday instances (MO, TU, etc). These instances may
            receive a parameter N, specifying the Nth weekday, which could
            be positive or negative (like MO(+1) or MO(-2). Not specifying
            it is the same as specifying +1. You can also use an integer,
            where 0=MO.

        leapdays:
            Will add given days to the date found, if year is a leap
            year, and the date found is post 28 of february.

        yearday, nlyearday:
            Set the yearday or the non-leap year day (jump leap days).

class relativedelta(object):
    """
    The relativedelta type is based on the specification of the excellent
    work done by M.-A. Lemburg in his
    `mx.DateTime <http://www.egenix.com/files/python/mxDateTime.html>`_ extension.
    However, notice that this type does *NOT* implement the same algorithm as
    his work. Do *NOT* expect it to behave like mx.DateTime's counterpart.

    There are two different ways to build a relativedelta instance. The
    first one is passing it two date/datetime classes::

        relativedelta(datetime1, datetime2)

    The second one is passing it any number of the following keyword arguments::

        relativedelta(arg1=x,arg2=y,arg3=z...)

        year, month, day, hour, minute, second, microsecond:
            Absolute information (argument is singular); adding or subtracting a
            relativedelta with absolute information does not perform an aritmetic
            operation, but rather REPLACES the corresponding value in the
            original datetime with the value(s) in relativedelta.

        years, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds, microseconds:
            Relative information, may be negative (argument is plural); adding
            or subtracting a relativedelta with relative information performs
            the corresponding aritmetic operation on the original datetime value
            with the information in the relativedelta.

        weekday:
            One of the weekday instances (MO, TU, etc). These instances may
            receive a parameter N, specifying the Nth weekday, which could
            be positive or negative (like MO(+1) or MO(-2). Not specifying
            it is the same as specifying +1. You can also use an integer,
            where 0=MO.

        leapdays:
            Will add given days to the date found, if year is a leap
            year, and the date found is post 28 of february.

        yearday, nlyearday:
            Set the yearday or the non-leap year day (jump leap days).
            These are converted to day/month/leapdays information.

    Here is the behavior of operations with relativedelta:

    1. Calculate the absolute year, using the 'year' argument, or the
       original datetime year, if the argument is not present.

    2. Add the relative 'years' argument to the absolute year.

    3. Do steps 1 and 2 for month/months.

    4. Calculate the absolute day, using the 'day' argument, or the
       original datetime day, if the argument is not present. Then,
       subtract from the day until it fits in the year and month
       found after their operations.

    5. Add the relative 'days' argument to the absolute day. Notice
       that the 'weeks' argument is multiplied by 7 and added to
       'days'.

    6. Do steps 1 and 2 for hour/hours, minute/minutes, second/seconds,
       microsecond/microseconds.

    7. If the 'weekday' argument is present, calculate the weekday,
       with the given (wday, nth) tuple. wday is the index of the
       weekday (0-6, 0=Mon), and nth is the number of weeks to add
       forward or backward, depending on its signal. Notice that if
       the calculated date is already Monday, for example, using
       (0, 1) or (0, -1) won't change the day.

# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
"""Regression tests: explicitly-set zero absolute values must survive
addition/subtraction of relativedelta objects.

The internal representation uses ``None`` for "not set" and ``0`` for
"explicitly set to zero", so merging with a truthiness test (``a or b``)
silently drops explicit zeros.
"""
from __future__ import unicode_literals
from ._common import unittest

from datetime import datetime

from dateutil.relativedelta import relativedelta

ABSOLUTE_ATTRS = ["year", "month", "day", "hour",
                  "minute", "second", "microsecond"]


class ZeroAbsoluteAdditionTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_add_zero_absolute_to_empty(self):
        # relativedelta() + relativedelta(day=0, hour=0)
        rd = relativedelta() + relativedelta(day=0, hour=0)
        self.assertIsNotNone(rd.day)
        self.assertIsNotNone(rd.hour)
        self.assertEqual(rd.day, 0)
        self.assertEqual(rd.hour, 0)
        self.assertEqual(rd, relativedelta(day=0, hour=0))

    def test_add_empty_to_zero_absolute(self):
        # relativedelta(day=0, hour=0) + relativedelta()
        rd = relativedelta(day=0, hour=0) + relativedelta()
        self.assertIsNotNone(rd.day)
        self.assertIsNotNone(rd.hour)
        self.assertEqual(rd.day, 0)
        self.assertEqual(rd.hour, 0)
        self.assertEqual(rd, relativedelta(day=0, hour=0))

    def test_all_absolute_attrs_zero_preserved_both_sides(self):
        for attr in ABSOLUTE_ATTRS:
            kwargs = {attr: 0}
            for rd in (relativedelta() + relativedelta(**kwargs),
                       relativedelta(**kwargs) + relativedelta(),
                       relativedelta(**kwargs).__radd__(relativedelta()),
                       sum([relativedelta(**kwargs), relativedelta()],
                           relativedelta())):
                self.assertIsNotNone(getattr(rd, attr),
                                     "%s lost in %r" % (attr, rd))
                self.assertEqual(getattr(rd, attr), 0, repr(rd))

    def test_unset_absolute_attrs_stay_none(self):
        rd = relativedelta() + relativedelta()
        for attr in ABSOLUTE_ATTRS:
            self.assertIsNone(getattr(rd, attr))
        self.assertFalse(rd)

        rd = relativedelta(months=1) + relativedelta(days=2)
        for attr in ABSOLUTE_ATTRS:
            self.assertIsNone(getattr(rd, attr))

    def test_zero_wins_over_unset_and_vice_versa(self):
        # An explicit zero must not be overwritten by an unset value.
        self.assertEqual((relativedelta() + relativedelta(day=0)).day, 0)
        self.assertEqual((relativedelta(day=0) + relativedelta()).day, 0)
        # An explicitly set non-zero value still takes precedence in __add__.
        self.assertEqual((relativedelta(day=5) + relativedelta(day=0)).day, 0)
        self.assertEqual((relativedelta(day=0) + relativedelta(day=5)).day, 5)

    def test_subtraction_keeps_zero(self):
        self.assertEqual((relativedelta(day=5) - relativedelta(day=0)).day, 5)
        self.assertEqual((relativedelta(day=0) - relativedelta(day=5)).day, 0)

    def test_normal_addition_unchanged(self):
        self.assertEqual(relativedelta(months=1) + relativedelta(days=2),
                         relativedelta(months=1, days=2))
        self.assertEqual(relativedelta(years=1, months=2) +
                         relativedelta(months=3, hours=4),
                         relativedelta(years=1, months=5, hours=4))
        self.assertEqual(relativedelta(year=2020, month=3) +
                         relativedelta(day=15),
                         relativedelta(year=2020, month=3, day=15))
        self.assertEqual(relativedelta(months=1) - relativedelta(days=2),
                         relativedelta(months=1, days=-2))

    def test_zero_time_absolute_applied_to_datetime(self):
        dt = datetime(2020, 5, 17, 13, 45, 30, 123456)
        self.assertEqual(dt + relativedelta(hour=0, minute=0,
                                            second=0, microsecond=0),
                         datetime(2020, 5, 17, 0, 0, 0))
        self.assertEqual(dt + relativedelta(), dt)

    def test_repr_keeps_zero(self):
        self.assertEqual(repr(relativedelta() + relativedelta(day=0, hour=0)),
                         "relativedelta(day=0, hour=0)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

## Bug fixed: `relativedelta + relativedelta` dropped explicitly-set zero absolute values

### Root cause
`relativedelta.__add__` (and `__sub__`) merged the singular absolute attributes with truthiness tests, e.g. `day=other.day or self.day`. Since the internal representation uses `None` for "not set" and `0` for "explicitly set to zero", an explicit `0` is falsy and was silently replaced by the other operand's value (or `None`). Same pattern for `year/month/day/weekday/hour/minute/second/microsecond` in both `__add__` and `__sub__` (lines ~318-338 and ~411-430).

### Files changed
1. `/dateutil/dateutil/relativedelta.py` — the fix (only source file I edited).
2. `/dateutil/dateutil/test/test_relativedelta_zero_absolute.py` — **new** regression test file (no existing test file was edited or deleted).

Note: the working tree already contained *pre-existing, unrelated* uncommitted edits before I started (`relativedelta.py` years/months `int()` normalization hunk, and `rrule.py` changes). I did not touch those; they show up in `git diff` but are not mine.

### Exact patch (my change only)
```diff
@@ relativedelta.__add__ (isinstance(other, relativedelta) branch)

-                                 hour=other.hour or self.hour,

-                                 second=other.second or self.second,
-                                 microsecond=(other.microsecond or
-                                              self.microsecond))
+                                 year=(other.year if other.year is not None
+                                       else self.year),
+                                 month=(other.month if other.month is not None
+                                        else self.month),
+                                 day=(other.day if other.day is not None
+                                      else self.day),
+                                 weekday=(other.weekday if other.weekday is not None
+                                          else self.weekday),

+                                       else self.hour),
+                                 minute=(other.minute if other.minute is not None
+                                         else self.minute),
+                                 second=(other.second if other.second is not None
+                                         else self.second),

+                                              if other.microsecond is not None
+                                              else self.microsecond))
@@ relativedelta.__sub__ (relativedelta - relativedelta branch)

-                             month=self.month or other.month,

-                             hour=self.hour or other.hour,
```

  - normal additions unchanged: `months=1 + days=2`, `years=1,months=2 + months=3,hours=4`, `year=2020,month=3 + day=15`, `months=1 - days=2`
  - applied to datetimes: `dt + relativedelta(hour=0, minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)` → `2020-05-17 00:00:00`

### Out of scope / known remaining `or`-guards (deliberately not changed)
`__add__`'s date-application path still uses `year = (self.year or other.year)+self.years`, `month = self.month or other.month`, `day = min(monthrange, self.day or other.day)` (lines ~359-371). Those are validity guards: `date.replace(day=0)` / `year=0` / `month=0` are invalid for real dates and would raise `ValueError`, so making them None-aware would be a behavior regression. Neither is caused by, nor fixed by, this change.
